summary: This RFC proposes enhancements to the Exterior Gateway Protocol for a simple multiple-level routing system called autonomous confederations. It generalizes the core system to include several communities of autonomous systems and asks for comments.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC asks how the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) could support more than one level of routing. It reinterprets the distance field that EGP already carries, so that paths inside your own network are always preferred over paths that leave it. The document asks for comments rather than setting a standard.

subtitle: One unused field in EGP, three routing levels, and no more dependence on a single core gateway system.

tldr.problem: Routing between networks in the early Internet relied on one central set of gateways, which was hard to administer and forced every network to reach that core directly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives the unused 8-bit distance field of the EGP Update message a three-level meaning: values below 128 for paths inside the sender's own system, 128 to 192 for paths inside its confederation, and 192 or more for everything else.
tldr.outcome: The document asks for discussion rather than setting a standard, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as unknown. No later RFC obsoletes it.

facts.label: Route choice
facts.value: The gateway with the minimum distance

today: RFC 975 is a 1986 proposal that asked for discussion and suggestions for improvement rather than specifying a standard, and the RFC Editor index lists its status as unknown. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a historical proposal for extending EGP.

sections.title: Why EGP Needed More Than One Routing Level
sections.content:
Internet exterior-gateway routing began with a rigid topological model that emphasized robustness and stability at the expense of routing dynamics and flexibility. The original model, suggested in RFC 827 and refined in RFC 888, restricted the Internet topology essentially to a tree whose root was the BBN-developed core gateway system.

The tree shape had one great advantage: routing loops between clusters of gateways, called autonomous systems, could not occur in it. Its disadvantages were the administrative and enforcement difficulties of running one core system, and the performance liabilities that came with it, which together made widespread implementation impractical.

EGP itself, documented in RFC 904, was an interim protocol with the capability of exchanging reachability information but not of functioning as a true routing algorithm, because no agreement could be reached on a trusted, common metric. As operational experience accumulated, it became clear that a more decentralized dynamic routing capability was needed to avoid resource-consuming suboptimal routes, and there was long-standing resistance to the assumption of a single core system with its implications for performance, administration, enforcement and subversion.
sections.plainLanguage: Early Internet routing between networks ran through one central set of gateways, which was hard to operate and forced every network to reach it. This RFC asks for a way to let groups of networks keep their own routing, using a field that EGP already carried but nobody had defined.

sections.title: The Routing Rules EGP Imposed
sections.content:
Only two restrictions are placed on a non-core gateway. A gateway can be listed in an EGP message only if it belongs to the same autonomous system, and a net can be listed only if it is reachable via gateways belonging to that system. There are no other restrictions, overt or implied. This third-party rule superseded earlier notions of stub systems or any other asymmetry.

The restrictions imply that, to ensure full connectivity, every non-core gateway must run EGP with a core gateway. Because the present core gateway implementation disallowed other gateways on EGP neighbour paths, every non-core gateway must also share a net in common with at least one core gateway.

There was no prior prohibition on using EGP as an interior gateway protocol, or on running EGP with a gateway of another non-core system, provided the third-party rule was observed. If a gateway in each system ran EGP with a gateway in every other system, the notion of a core system would be unnecessary and superfluous.
sections.plainLanguage: EGP let a gateway report only the networks it could reach itself, not the networks it had heard about from a third gateway. That rule kept routing loops away, but it also meant every network needed a direct link to the single core system.

sections.title: Autonomous Systems and Confederations
sections.content:
An autonomous system is a set of gateways, each of which can reach any other gateway in the same system using paths that go only through gateways of that system. The gateways cooperate to maintain a routing data base using an interior gateway protocol (IGP), and that IGP is expected to include security mechanisms so that only gateways of the same system can acquire each other as neighbours.

An autonomous confederation is a set of autonomous systems that share a common security model, meaning that they trust each other to compute routes to other systems in the same confederation. Each gateway in a confederation can reach any other gateway in it using paths only inside the confederation. The RFC expects some mechanism to let potential EGP neighbours discover whether they are in the same confederation, for example access control lists or a partitioning of the set of system numbers.

A network is directly reachable from an autonomous system when a gateway in that system has an interface to it, and reachable when it is directly reachable from a system belonging to the same confederation. Every gateway in a confederation is entitled to list all reachable nets in the EGP messages it sends to any other system.
sections.plainLanguage: An autonomous confederation is a set of separate networks that trust each other to compute routes. Inside such a group, a gateway may pass on what it learned from another member's gateway, because the group trusts that gateway's information.

sections.title: A Three-Level Distance Metric
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a general observation about distributed systems: the nearer a thing is, the more dynamic and trustable it is, while the farther away it is, the more static and suspicious it becomes. Neighbouring gateways exchange detailed information with a fast algorithm, while widely separated systems need only coarse hints, require more elaborate security, and can afford less frequent updates.

The metric is therefore an integer in which low values mean near and high values mean far. Values less than a globally agreed constant X are associated with paths confined to the same autonomous system as the sender, values greater than X but less than another constant Y with paths confined to the sender's confederation, and values greater than Y with the remaining paths. For illustration, the RFC takes X to be 128 and Y to be 192.

At each of the three levels, autonomous system, autonomous confederation and universe of confederations, several routing algorithms could run at once, each producing a possibly different subtree and metric for every destination net. Within a system the metric must have the same interpretation so that other systems can mediate routes between its gateways, and the same holds within a confederation. All confederations must agree on a common universe-of-confederations algorithm, but the confederation-level and system-level algorithms may differ from group to group.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives the distance field three bands. Small values mean the path stays inside your own network, middle values mean it stays inside your confederation, and large values mean it leaves both. A gateway always takes the lowest band available, so it prefers its own network first.

sections.title: How a Gateway Stores and Updates Routes
sections.content:
The routing table holds a net number and a list of items. Each item carries the gateway address, system number and distance provided by an EGP neighbour, a time-to-live counter, and local routing information.

When an EGP Update message arrives, the gateway decodes it into quads of network number, gateway address, system number and distance. If the gateway address is internal to the neighbour's system, the quad keeps that system number; otherwise the system number is set to zero, meaning external. A new distance is then computed. If the system number matches the local system number, the rules of the system IGP apply but the value must be less than 128. If the system is in the same confederation, or the system number is zero and the old distance was less than 192, the confederation rules apply and the value must be at least 128 and less than 192. Otherwise the universe-of-confederations rules apply and the value must be at least 192.

The time-to-live field of every item is incremented regularly. An item that passes a preset maximum is discarded, and when all items for a net are gone the whole entry goes with them. To send an Update, the gateway inverts its table by gateway address, selects the gateway with the minimum distance for each net, sorts the result by gateway address and partitions it on internal and external system number.
sections.plainLanguage: Each gateway keeps a routing table: a list of networks, and for each one the gateways that can reach it, with a distance and a timer. When an EGP update arrives, the gateway rewrites the distances into the right band and drops entries whose timer runs out.

sections.title: Working with Existing EGP Implementations
sections.content:
The proposed interpretation is backwards compatible with known EGP implementations that do not interpret the distance field, and with several known implementations that take private liberties with it. No retrofit is needed in existing implementations for them to interoperate with enhanced implementations.

The simplest way to evolve the present system is to collect the existing implementations that ignore the distance field into a single confederation with the present core system and its routing restrictions. All distances provided by that confederation would be assumed equal to 192, which gives at least a rudimentary capability for routing within the universe of confederations.

Systems in which the distance field already has a uniform interpretation, such as the Butterfly gateways then being deployed, can be organized as autonomous confederations of their own. Their distance fields can be set to at least 128 when the routing information comes from another member of the same group, and to at least 192 when it comes from a system presumed to be outside it. The three-level hierarchy could be extended to more levels, but the distance field in the current EGP model is limited to eight bits, and each extra level would put more strain on it.
sections.plainLanguage: The change needs no work in existing EGP software, because the distance field had no agreed meaning before. A network that ignores the field can simply be treated as one more member of the group around the core system.

viz.caption: THE THREE LEVELS OF THE EGP DISTANCE FIELD

cells: The path stays inside the sender's own system.
The path stays inside the sender's confederation.
The path leaves the sender's system and its confederation.
